definition: In psychology, game theory, statistics, and machine learning, win–stay, lose–switch (also win–stay, lose–shift or Pavlov, named after Ivan Pavlov) is a heuristic learning strategy used to model learning in decision situations.
details: It was first invented as an improvement over randomization in bandit problems. It was later applied to the prisoner's dilemma in order to model the evolution of altruism. In most versions, it starts either with a cooperate, then proceeds as always, or starts with a "probe" of cooperate-defect-cooperate to determine the other player's strategy. A mutual cooperation is regarded as a win. The learning rule bases its decision only on the outcome of the previous play. Outcomes are divided into successes (wins) and failures (losses). If the play on the previous round resulted in a success, then the agent plays the same strategy on the next round. Alternatively, if the play resulted in a failure the agent switches to another action. A large-scale empirical study of players of the game rock, paper, scissors shows that a variation of this strategy is adopted by real-world players of the game, instead of the Nash equilibrium strategy of choosing entirely at random between the three options.

explainer.lead: Win–stay, lose–switch (also Pavlov) is a heuristic learning strategy that repeats an action after success and changes it after failure. It matters in psychology, game theory, statistics and machine learning as a model of learning in repeated decisions.

tiers.eli5: If something worked, do it again; if it didn't, try something different next time.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a simple rule in repeated games and bandit problems. A pitfall is its narrowness: decisions rest only on the outcome of the previous play, so it can be slow to adapt to changing conditions.
tiers.paperLevel: A learning heuristic that bases its next decision only on the previous play's outcome, with outcomes classed as successes or failures. It was invented as an improvement over randomization in bandit problems and later applied to the prisoner's dilemma to model the evolution of altruism.

explainer.example: A player cooperates, treats mutual cooperation as a win, and keeps cooperating; after a loss it switches its move.
